section.title: Lord of the Sabbath
section.sectionRationale: Conflict with the Pharisees now hardens around the Sabbath. When they accuse His disciples of unlawful reaping and then watch to trap Him over healing, Jesus answers from Scripture, declares Himself Lord of the Sabbath, and does good by restoring a withered hand. As the plot to kill Him forms, Matthew presents Jesus through Isaiah as the gentle, chosen Servant in whom the nations will hope.
section.thesis: As Lord of the Sabbath, greater than the temple, Jesus reclaims the day for mercy and doing good over rigid legalism, and even as His enemies plot His death He fulfills Isaiah's portrait of the gentle Servant who will not break the bruised reed but will bring justice to victory and hope to the nations.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the grainfields and the declaration that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath; the healing of the withered hand and the plot to kill Him; and the fulfillment of Isaiah's gentle Servant who brings hope to the nations.

verses.text: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the {{sabbaton|Sabbath}}. His disciples were hungry and began to pick the heads of grain and eat them.
When the Pharisees saw this, they said to Him, “Look, Your disciples are doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath.”
Jesus replied, “Have you not read what David did when he and his companions were hungry?
He entered the house of God, and he and his companions ate the consecrated bread, which was not lawful for them to eat, but only for the priests.
Or haven’t you read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are innocent?
But I tell you that One greater than the temple is here.
If only you had known the meaning of ‘I desire {{eleos|mercy}}, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent.
For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
Moving on from there, Jesus entered their synagogue,
and a man with a withered hand was there. In order to accuse Jesus, they asked Him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”
He replied, “If one of you has a sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will he not take hold of it and lift it out?
How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.”
Then Jesus said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored to full use, just like the other.
But the Pharisees went out and plotted how they might kill Jesus.

units.label: God's chosen Servant
units.note: a bruised reed He will not break

verses.text: Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place. Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all,
warning them not to make Him known.
This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah:
“Here is My {{pais|Servant}}, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim {{krisis|justice}} to the nations.
He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets.
A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory.
In His name the nations will put their hope.”

sabbaton.gloss: Sabbath, the seventh-day rest commanded in the law. The Pharisees had fenced it with detailed rules; Jesus reclaims its true purpose as a gift for mercy and doing good, and claims lordship over it as the Son of Man.

eleos.gloss: Mercy, compassion, covenant kindness. Quoting Hosea 6:6 again, Jesus insists that God prizes mercy over ritual precision; had the Pharisees grasped this, they would not have condemned His hungry, innocent disciples.

pais.gloss: Servant, also son or child. In the Isaiah quotation it names the LORD's chosen Servant, beloved and Spirit-anointed; Matthew identifies Jesus as this gentle Servant who brings justice to the nations.

krisis.gloss: Justice, judgment, right ruling. The Servant proclaims and finally establishes God's justice, not by force or clamor but by gentle faithfulness, leading justice to victory and giving the nations hope in His name.

basic.context: On the Sabbath, Jesus' hungry disciples pick heads of grain, and the Pharisees accuse them of breaking the law. Jesus answers with Scripture, David eating the holy bread, priests working in the temple, and Hosea's word that God desires mercy, then declares Himself Lord of the Sabbath. In the synagogue He heals a man's withered hand, insisting it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. The Pharisees plot to kill Him, and Matthew presents Him as Isaiah's gentle Servant.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the Sabbath conflicts as clashes over the meaning of the law. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath but exposes the Pharisees' additions and recovers its true purpose: mercy and doing good. His claim to be Lord of the Sabbath is a claim to divine authority. The Isaiah quotation interprets His withdrawal and gentleness as the fulfillment of the Servant prophecy, not weakness.
basic.originalLanguages: The Sabbath was God's gift, but the Pharisees had buried it under rules. Jesus quotes Hosea: God desires mercy, not mere sacrifice. Matthew names Jesus the chosen Servant of Isaiah, the beloved Spirit-anointed one who brings God's justice to the nations, not by clamor but by gentleness, till He leads justice to victory.
basic.typology: David eating the consecrated bread and the priests working on the Sabbath foreshadow a greater one whose presence reorders the old order: one greater than the temple is here. And Isaiah's Servant, gentle with the bruised reed, is fulfilled in Jesus, whose quiet, merciful ministry carries hope to the Gentiles.
basic.christ: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and greater than the temple, the one to whom the day and its rest belong. He is the gentle Servant of Isaiah, chosen and beloved, who will not crush the weak or snuff out the faint but tenderly restores them. And He is the hope of the nations, bringing God's justice to final victory.
basic.god: God desires mercy, not mere ritual; His law was always meant to serve love and life. He delights in His chosen Servant and puts His Spirit on Him. And His purpose reaches beyond Israel to the nations, who will put their hope in the Servant's name, showing a God whose salvation is for the world.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 21 tells of David and the consecrated bread. Hosea 6:6 is quoted, mercy not sacrifice. Isaiah 42:1-4 is the Servant Song Matthew cites in full. And Hebrews 4 presents the true Sabbath rest that Jesus gives His people.
basic.oneStory: The conflict over the Sabbath reveals who Jesus is: the Lord of the day, greater than the temple, come to restore mercy over crushing legalism. Even as opposition hardens into a death plot, He does not rage or retaliate but fulfills Isaiah's gentle Servant, tender with the bruised and faint, carrying God's justice and hope out to the nations. The quiet Servant on His way to the cross is the world's only hope.

context.literary:
Matthew 12 begins with the words at that time, tying it to the invitation that closed chapter 11. Jesus has just offered rest to the weary, and the very next scene is a dispute about rest. The order is deliberate. Matthew shows that the offer of rest and the dispute about the Sabbath are two views of one question: who is the Lord who gives rest, and what is the day for?

The passage has three panels. The first, verses 1 to 8, is a controversy story, with a charge, a counter-argument in three steps and a declaration. The second, verses 9 to 14, is a healing in a synagogue framed as a controversy, with a trap question, an argument from a sheep and a deed. The third, verses 15 to 21, is a summary of Jesus' withdrawal and healing, followed by a long quotation from Isaiah. The panels build upon one another: the first claims authority, the second displays it in mercy, and the third shows from Scripture what kind of authority this is. The plot that ends the second panel, verse 14, drives the third, because the withdrawal in verse 15 is a response to it.

The counter-argument in verses 3 to 7 is carefully built. Each of the three steps begins with a question about reading, have you not read, or haven't you read in the Law, and the third is an appeal to a prophet, if you had known. The first draws on the narrative of David, the second on the Law and the third on the Prophets, so that all three divisions of the Scriptures are brought in. The first two cases concern permitted breaches of a rule, and the second also includes the claim that something greater than the temple is here. Verses 6 to 8 then turn the argument on a single person: greater than the temple, Lord of the Sabbath.

The Isaiah quotation is placed at the end so that it can interpret everything before it. The one who seemed to break a law and who was hunted by a plot is the chosen Servant, and Matthew reads the whole conflict in the light of Isaiah 42. The echoes of earlier chapters in this quotation are deliberate: the voice of the Father at the baptism, the Spirit upon Him, the bruised reed that recalls the reed of chapter 11, and the hope of the nations.
context.historical:
By the first century the Sabbath had become one of the main marks of Jewish identity, and it was guarded with detailed rules. The Law forbade work on the seventh day, Exodus 20:8-11 and Deuteronomy 5:12-15, and it called the Sabbath a sign of the covenant, Exodus 31:13-17. Exodus 16:23-30 had already shown that gathering food was a kind of work to be avoided, and in the exile and after it the prophets and Nehemiah had treated Sabbath-breaking as a cause of the nation's downfall, Jeremiah 17:21-22 and Nehemiah 13:15-18. A people that had lost its land because of such sins was understandably careful to build a fence around the day.

The charge in verse 2 does not say that the disciples stole. The Law allowed hungry travellers to pluck heads of grain from a neighbour's field, Deuteronomy 23:25. The offence alleged is the act of plucking on the Sabbath, which could be classed as reaping. This is why the question is whether it is lawful, and why Jesus answers by turning to Scripture and not to tradition.

David's visit to Nob is told in 1 Samuel 21:1-6. The consecrated bread, the bread of the Presence, was set out as twelve loaves each Sabbath and then eaten by the priests in a holy place, Leviticus 24:5-9. Matthew drops the high priest's name that Mark gives, and Mark 2:26 names Abiathar where 1 Samuel 21:1 names Ahimelech, a small difference that Matthew's shorter form avoids. David's case is strong because he was not a priest, he was in need and the holy bread was given to him. Jesus' point does not depend on the details of the incident but on the fact that the Scriptures themselves record a case of human need taking precedence over a ritual rule.

The priests' work on the Sabbath is also well established. Numbers 28:9-10 required two extra lambs on the Sabbath, and the showbread was replaced weekly, 1 Chronicles 9:32. The temple was a place where Sabbath labour was commanded. Jesus' argument is that if the temple's service outweighs the Sabbath rule, then what is greater than the temple does so all the more.

The man in the synagogue had a withered hand. A common view of the time was that healing was permitted on the Sabbath only when life was in danger, and the question in verse 10 puts Jesus in the position of having to choose between a rule and a need. Jesus' sheep argument appeals to a practice that his hearers already allowed, and that the Law implies elsewhere, Deuteronomy 22:4 and Exodus 23:4-5. The plot in verse 14 shows that the response was not debate but a conspiracy, and Mark 3:6 adds that the Herodians joined it.
context.canonical:
The Sabbath begins at creation, where God rested on the seventh day, blessed it and sanctified it, Genesis 2:2-3. It is renewed in the Ten Commandments with two reasons attached: the rest of the Creator, Exodus 20:11, and the memory of slavery in Egypt, Deuteronomy 5:15. Jesus' approach honours both reasons. The day is for rest and for the freedom that God gave His people, and it is a gift to the weary, including the servants and animals, Exodus 23:12. The Sabbath is also a sign of the covenant, Ezekiel 20:12, and Isaiah 58:13-14 shows what it can be when it is kept as a delight rather than a burden.

The use of Hosea 6:6, I desire mercy, not sacrifice, is the second in Matthew. Jesus has already said it at the table with tax collectors in Matthew 9:13, and He tells His critics there to go and learn what it means. Here He says they would not have condemned the innocent if they had known. The prophet's word is a standing summary of what God wants from His people, with chesed, steadfast love, set above the machinery of sacrifice, and the same point returns in Matthew 23:23, where the weightier matters of the law are justice, mercy and faithfulness.

Isaiah 42:1-4 is the first of the Servant Songs. Matthew quotes it in his own form, close to the Greek translation, and the Servant of the song is the one who brings justice to the nations. The song was read by the early church as a portrait of Jesus. The voice at the baptism, This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, Matthew 3:17, and at the Transfiguration, Matthew 17:5, uses the same language of beloved and delight, and links the Servant with the Son. The Servant's mission to the nations continues in Isaiah 49:6, which Paul and Barnabas apply to their own mission in Acts 13:47, and in the hope of the Root of Jesse in Isaiah 11:10, quoted in Romans 15:12.

The New Testament carries the Sabbath question forward in several ways. Hebrews 4:9 says that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. Colossians 2:16-17 calls the Sabbath a shadow of things to come whose substance belongs to Christ, and Romans 14:5-6 treats the observance of days as a matter of conviction before the Lord. The early church met on the first day of the week, Acts 20:7, and John speaks of the Lord's day, Revelation 1:10. Whatever one makes of the details, all these texts hold that the Sabbath finds its meaning in Christ.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew writes for readers who were still being told by synagogue authorities that Jesus' followers were lawbreakers, and for Jewish Christians who loved the Torah and wondered how to read it now. His answer is not that the Law has been set aside, but that its true meaning has been disclosed in Jesus. He gathers three Scriptural arguments, from David, from the temple service and from Hosea, to show that the Law itself already allowed mercy and need to outweigh a rule, so that Jesus is not an innovator but a faithful reader.

He also wants his readers to see the authority of Jesus. The claim in verse 6 and verse 8 is not a minor adjustment of a rule; it is a claim to be above the temple and the Sabbath, the two great institutions of Israel's worship. No mere interpreter could say it. The author intends the hearer to stop and face the question, who is this?

The Isaiah quotation is meant to reshape what readers expect of such authority. A reader who has just seen conflict and a murderous plot might expect the Messiah to answer with force. Matthew shows instead a Servant who withdraws, who heals everyone who comes, who does not shout, and who will not crush the fragile. The author is answering a quiet question that the church faced, why does the Messiah suffer opposition and not triumph at once, and he does it from the Scriptures: it was foretold, and gentleness is the form His power takes.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The incidents describe what Jesus and His disciples did on particular Sabbaths and how He answered the charges. They do not tell believers to pick grain in other people's fields, nor do they cancel the principle of rest. What the passage shows is how to read a command: with attention to the purpose God gave it, and with mercy for the person it serves. The Sabbath was given for rest, and the answer to a rule used to withhold relief is the rule's own purpose.

The decisive statements are descriptive of Jesus. He is greater than the temple and Lord of the Sabbath; these are claims about Him, not instructions for His followers. They do not give believers authority to set the Sabbath aside, but they explain why the question of the Sabbath must be answered in relation to Him.

There is also prescription in the passage. Verse 7 tells readers what to know: that God desires mercy. Verse 12 states a general principle, that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. These apply today to anyone who uses religious rules to avoid acts of kindness, and they apply as well to those who use the language of mercy to dismiss God's commands. The passage does not give permission to treat rest as optional, since Jesus Himself is the one who offers rest, and it does not tell the church how to observe particular days. Other Scriptures take up that question, and believers differ in how they apply them.

debates.question: Did Jesus break the Sabbath, or reveal its true meaning?

views.label: He recovered its God-intended purpose
views.case: Jesus rejects not the Sabbath but the Pharisees' burdensome additions, showing from Scripture that mercy and doing good were always its aim; the day was made for man's blessing, not his bondage.

views.label: He exercised divine lordship over it
views.case: As the Son of Man who is Lord of the Sabbath, Jesus has authority over the day itself; His actions are not violations but the rightful ordering of the Sabbath by the One to whom it belongs.

debates.bearing: Both affirm that Jesus honors the law's true intent and claims an authority only its divine Author could hold, so the Sabbath finds its meaning and rest in Him.

debates.question: How does the gentle Servant of Isaiah 42 shape our picture of Jesus?

views.label: Gentleness with the weak and broken
views.case: The Servant will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick, portraying Jesus' tender care for the fragile and faltering, the very opposite of the Pharisees' harshness.

views.label: Quiet, certain triumph of justice
views.case: The same Servant will lead justice to victory and give the nations hope; His gentleness is not weakness but the manner of a King whose reign will surely prevail.

debates.bearing: Both hold together the tenderness and the triumph of Christ: He is gentle with the weak and unstoppable in bringing God's justice and hope to the world.

debates.question: What does the Sabbath mean for Christians today?

views.label: The principle continues, observed on the Lord's day
views.case: Many in the Reformed and Puritan tradition hold that the commandment rests on creation and continues, with the day shifted to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection, Acts 20:7 and Revelation 1:10. Jesus corrects the abuses of the day but does not abolish it.

views.label: The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ
views.case: Others point to Colossians 2:16-17, where the Sabbath is a shadow whose substance is Christ, and to Hebrews 4:9-10, where rest is entered by faith. On this view the weekly day is no longer binding, though believers still need rhythms of rest and worship, and Romans 14:5-6 leaves the observance of days to conscience.

views.label: The seventh day itself remains
views.case: A smaller group holds that the commandment was never moved, and that Jesus' own keeping of the seventh day and His correction of its abuses show that it stands. They read the passage as a recovery of the day's purpose, not an end of the day.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on what this passage shows: that the Sabbath was made for human good, that mercy and doing good are always lawful, and that Jesus is the Lord to whom the day belongs. They differ on the weekly application, and the New Testament leaves room for the discussion.

study.originalLanguages:
The question that frames the argument is ouk anegnote, have you not read, which appears twice in verses 3 and 5. Jesus' critics were men who read the Scriptures daily, and the question is a sharp one for them. It suggests that the problem is not a lack of text but a failure to hear it. In verse 7 the charge sharpens: if you had known, egnokeite, what it means. The shift from reading to knowing is the shift from the surface of the text to its heart.

Verse 6 says that something greater than the temple is here. The Greek word is meizon, a neuter form of the comparative, literally a greater thing, and in 12:41 and 12:42 Matthew uses a similar neuter, more than Jonah and more than Solomon is here. English versions differ on whether to render it as a person or a thing. The neuter leaves the claim open for a moment, a greater something, and then verse 8 names the person: the Son of Man is the Lord of the Sabbath. The word kyrios, lord, is the word the Greek Bible uses for the LORD, and the claim is placed in the mouth of the Son of Man, the title taken from Daniel 7:13-14.

The quotation from Hosea 6:6 reads eleos thelo kai ou thysian, I desire mercy and not sacrifice. The Hebrew word behind mercy is chesed, the covenant love and loyalty that runs through the Old Testament, and the verse goes on to say that God desires the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. Jesus quotes the first half and the second half hangs on it: the knowledge of God is what the critics are missing. Those they condemn are anaitious, guiltless or blameless, a term that means no charge can be brought against them.

The healing of the hand is described with care. The hand is xeran, dried up or withered, and Jesus says ekteinon, stretch out. The man ekteinen, stretched it out, and the hand was apekatestathe, restored. The verb is apokathistemi, to restore to a former state, and Matthew uses its future form in 17:11, where Elijah will restore all things. The healing is a small act of restoration of the kind that Jesus announces as the work of the coming age.

The plot of verse 14 is that the Pharisees symboulion elabon, took counsel, a phrase Matthew uses for formal consultations that end in a plan, including the plan against Jesus in 27:1. The word for plotting is not a casual remark. It marks the point at which opposition becomes a plan, and verse 15 says that Jesus, knowing it, anechoresen, withdrew. The verb is Matthew's habitual one for a strategic retreat, used in 4:12 and 14:13.

The Isaiah quotation has several Greek features worth noticing. The Servant is ho pais mou, a phrase that can mean My servant or My child, and the same Greek word covers both. He is ho agapetos mou, My beloved, the word used at the baptism, 3:17, and the verb for delight, eudokeo, is the same as in the heavenly voice. The Spirit is put upon Him as it descended at the baptism. The bruised reed is kalamon syntetrimmenon, and the word for reed, kalamos, appeared in 11:7 when Jesus asked the crowd whether John was a reed shaken by the wind. The smouldering wick is linon typhomenon, a flax wick smoking and nearly out. Finally, Jesus will ekbale justice to victory, using the same verb as for driving out demons and sending out workers, 9:38 and 12:28. Justice is not coaxed into the world; it is thrust out and carried to victory. The last line, in His name the nations will hope, follows the Greek translation of Isaiah, which reads name where the Hebrew behind the BSB reads law.

typology.type: David and the bread of the Presence
typology.fulfillment: David, the anointed king on the run, ate the bread that only priests might eat, because he and his men were hungry, 1 Samuel 21:4-6. Jesus draws on the story to show that the rule of the holy bread yielded to a greater thing, the need of the Lord's anointed and His company. The correspondence is that Jesus is the Son of David, and the hungry disciples are His companions. The escalation is that David was a king by promise and yet fled, while Jesus is the king in His own right and His authority extends to the Sabbath itself. Where David depended on a priest's permission, Jesus is the one who gives it. The type falls short because David took holy things for a day, while Christ will become the bread that gives life to the world, John 6:35.

The priests worked on the Sabbath in the temple service, Numbers 28:9-10, and were innocent because the temple's work took precedence. Jesus says that something greater than the temple is here, and the temple, the place where God dwelt among His people, was always a sign of His presence. In Jesus the presence is a person, as John 1:14 says the Word made His dwelling among us. He also spoke of the temple of His body, John 2:19-21, and the veil was torn at His death, Matthew 27:51. The church is now built into a holy temple in Him, Ephesians 2:21-22. The type falls short because the temple was a building, set apart in one place, while Christ is present everywhere that His people gather.

The Sabbath looked back to the rest of God at creation and forward to a rest that Israel never fully entered, as Hebrews 4:8-9 argues. Jesus, who has just invited the weary to come to Him for rest, now claims to be Lord of the day. The correspondence is that the weekly rest was a promise of a greater rest. The escalation is that rest is found in a person, and Colossians 2:17 says the substance belongs to Christ. The type is not abolished in its purpose, for Hebrews 4:9 says a rest remains, and it will be complete only when the work of redemption is complete, Revelation 14:13.

typology.type: The gentle Servant of the LORD
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 42:1-4 describes a Servant who is chosen, upheld by the LORD, endowed with the Spirit and charged with bringing justice to the nations. Matthew shows Jesus as this Servant, who withdraws before His enemies and heals the crowds, who does not shout and who treats the weak with care. The same Servant is the one who will suffer, Isaiah 53:11-12. The escalation is that the gentleness is not a defect but a mode of strength, since the Servant will not grow weak or discouraged until justice is established. The type is still unfolding, because the justice has been carried to victory in the cross and resurrection but will be revealed completely only when He returns.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by the weight of the claims He makes. In the space of three verses He says that something greater than the temple is here and that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath. The temple was the house of God and the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant, and no prophet had set himself above either. The claim fits John 5:17-18, where Jesus says that His Father is at work and that He is too, and where the opponents understood that He was making Himself equal with God. Here Matthew gives the same claim from the side of Scripture: the Lord of the day is the one who made it, and the one who made it for rest is the one who offers rest.

He is also the Son of David. The argument from David is not a rabbinic trick but a claim about who Jesus is. David was the anointed king, and when he was in need, he was given what was holy. Jesus is the son of that David, and the one promised in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 to have an everlasting throne. The disciples are the companions of that King, and their need, in His presence, is a holy thing. The point is made not by mere analogy but by the identity of the one who is speaking.

The quotation from Isaiah brings the Servant forward. Matthew places it at the point where Jesus withdraws from a plot to kill Him, and in so doing he shows that the withdrawal is part of the divine plan and not a defeat. The Servant is chosen, beloved and anointed, and He will bring justice to the nations. The first line echoes the voice from heaven at the baptism, and the Spirit upon Him is the Spirit who descended there. He is the Father's beloved, and His gentleness is the Father's own. The Servant whom Isaiah describes goes on to be oppressed and afflicted, and to bear the sin of many, Isaiah 53:11-12, so the quiet withdrawal of chapter 12 points toward the cross.

Within the passage, His authority and His gentleness belong together. He heals the withered hand with a word, and He withdraws and does not cry out. He lifts the fallen sheep and will not break the bruised reed. The same Lord who stands above the Sabbath is the one who stoops to a man with a useless hand. The contrast between His critics and Himself is stark: they are concerned to guard the day; He is concerned to restore the person. And He will lead justice to victory, which means the matter does not end with the gentleness but with the triumph that gentleness brings.

The nations are in view from the first. The Servant proclaims justice to the Gentiles and in His name they hope. Paul uses the same phrase in Romans 15:12 and Acts 13:47 to describe the mission to the Gentiles, and Matthew's own gospel will end with the nations being made disciples. The one who seemed to break the law is the one in whom the whole world will place its hope.

A caution applies. The grainfield is not a coded picture of the church, and the withered hand is not a hidden allegory of Israel. The links above rest on what Jesus says here about Himself and on the Isaiah text that Matthew himself cites.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that the Sabbath is His gift. It is not a burden placed on people by a harsh ruler but a provision for their rest, grounded in His own resting at creation, Genesis 2:2-3, and in His rescue of Israel from slavery, Deuteronomy 5:15. The Pharisees treat the day as something to be protected from human need; God treats it as something given to meet human need. The passage is a sharp reminder that the God of the Law is the God of mercy, and that He tells His people so, Hosea 6:6.

He is the God who desires mercy. The verse that Jesus quotes does not say that God dislikes sacrifice, since sacrifice is part of His command, but that He desires something more basic, the covenant loyalty and love of a people who know Him. The doctrine of God here is one in which holiness and mercy do not compete. A God who is holy requires sacrifice, and a God who is love prefers mercy, and the two come together in Christ. Those who think that strictness is a way of honouring God are shown that honouring Him means doing what He loves.

He is also the God who acts in His Son. Verse 18 is a Trinitarian text: the Father speaks of the Servant as chosen and beloved, in whom His soul delights, and says that He will put His Spirit on Him. The three are in relation, and each has a part. The Father chooses and delights, the Son serves, the Spirit rests upon Him. It is the same picture as the baptism in 3:16-17, and it grounds the mission of Jesus in the love of the Father and the power of the Spirit. The Son's gentleness is not a different thing from the Father's heart; it is the shape the Father's heart takes when He comes among us.

He is the God whose justice is gentle and certain. The Servant will bring forth justice, and the verb implies that it is not left to chance. He will not be discouraged or grow weak, Isaiah 42:4, and He will lead justice to victory. There is no tension in Matthew between the gentle Servant and the powerful King. The God who looks after a smouldering wick is the God who sees that justice triumphs, and the nations will hope in His name.

For worship, the passage asks us to come to God without fear of His commands being a trap. His day is a gift, His law is for life, and His Son is a refuge for the weak. It also asks us to guard against making religion a way of avoiding the neighbour. We worship the God who is Lord of the Sabbath by seeking what pleases Him, and what pleases Him is mercy.

crossReferences.note: David comes to Nob and receives the consecrated bread, because there is no common bread, and the priest gives it to him and his men. Jesus' reference to it presses the point that the Law itself records a case where need and the Lord's anointed took precedence over a ritual rule.

The twelve loaves of the bread of the Presence were set out on the table every Sabbath and were to be eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place. Knowing this makes David's act more striking and shows that the Sabbath itself was marked by the presence of holy bread.

The Law commands extra offerings on the Sabbath. It is the Scriptural basis for Jesus' claim that the priests break the Sabbath in the temple and are innocent, and it shows that Sabbath work was written into the Law itself.

God desires mercy and the knowledge of God rather than sacrifice and burnt offerings. Jesus uses it to say that the critics have missed the heart of the Law, and He has already used it in Matthew 9:13. The verse sets the purpose of the Law against its misuse.

The fourth commandment grounds the Sabbath in the rest of the Creator and extends it to servants, foreigners and animals. It shows the generosity of the day's purpose and explains why Jesus can speak of it as a gift to be used for good.

The second giving of the commandment grounds the Sabbath in the memory of slavery in Egypt, so that the day is a day of release as well as rest. It helps explain why Jesus sees the freeing of a man from a withered hand as in keeping with the day.

Mark's version adds that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and names Abiathar as high priest. Reading it beside Matthew shows that Matthew has chosen to stress the priests and the temple, with the argument about the temple and mercy that Mark does not contain.

Jesus heals a woman bent over for eighteen years on a Sabbath and answers the synagogue leader with the example of the ox and the donkey led to water. It is a companion to Matthew's sheep in the pit, and it shows that the pattern recurs in His ministry.

Jesus answers the charge of Sabbath-breaking by saying that His Father is at work to this very day and He is also working. His opponents see in it a claim of equality with God, and so it shows what lies behind the title Lord of the Sabbath.

The first Servant Song, quoted in Matthew 12:18-21. The Servant is chosen and Spirit-endowed, will not cry out, will not break a bruised reed and will establish justice in the earth. It supplies the picture by which Matthew reads the withdrawal of Jesus and His healing of the crowds.

The voice from heaven calls Jesus My beloved Son in whom I am well pleased. Matthew's quotation of Isaiah uses the same two ideas for the Servant, beloved and delight, so that the baptism and the Servant Song interpret each other.

Paul calls Sabbaths a shadow of the things to come, whose substance belongs to Christ. It shows how the apostles took Jesus' claim to be Lord of the Sabbath, and it is the text at the centre of Christian discussion of the Sabbath.

study.oneStory:
The Sabbath is the first thing God makes holy. Before Eden is lost, before any law is given, God blesses the seventh day and rests, Genesis 2:2-3. The day is built into creation as a sign that the world is meant to end in rest and not in endless labour. When sin enters the story, work becomes toil, Genesis 3:17-19, and rest becomes something to be recovered. The Sabbath keeps alive the memory of what was meant and the hope of what will be restored.

The commandment is given to a people just freed from slavery, and Deuteronomy 5:15 ties it to that freedom. The long history of Israel's failure to keep the Sabbath, in Jeremiah 17 and Nehemiah 13, is part of the story of exile, and the land itself enjoyed its Sabbaths while the people were away, 2 Chronicles 36:21. So when the Pharisees in Matthew 12 guard the day with such care, they are acting in light of a history in which the loss of the Sabbath meant the loss of the land. What Jesus does is address both the memory and the hope: He does not belittle the history, and He shows what the day was always for.

The passage sets up the rest of the gospel. The plot of verse 14 begins the road to the cross, and the Servant who withdraws is the Servant who will be led like a lamb to the slaughter, Isaiah 53:7. The fuller opposition of Matthew 12:22 and following, with its charge that He works by Beelzebul, grows out of this scene. And the Servant's hope for the nations is carried through to the Great Commission in 28:19.

The rest that the Sabbath promises is the rest that will be completed. Hebrews 4:9 says that there remains a Sabbath rest, and Revelation 14:13 speaks of those who die in the Lord resting from their labours. In the new creation, the work of redemption is done, the people of God are at home with their Lord, and the nations walk by His light, Revelation 21:24. The Lord of the Sabbath, who as Servant did not break a bruised reed, brings His people into that rest and leads justice to victory, and the weary rest because the work has been finished.

quiz.q: How did Jesus respond to the charge that His disciples broke the Sabbath by picking grain?

options.text: He appealed to Scripture and declared that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
options.note: Verses 3-8 cite David, the priests, and Hosea, and claim lordship over the Sabbath.

options.text: He admitted they had sinned but asked for mercy.
options.note: He defended them as innocent, not guilty, and claimed authority over the Sabbath.

options.text: He said the Sabbath command no longer applied to anyone.
options.note: He did not abolish the Sabbath; He recovered its purpose and claimed lordship over it.

options.text: He rebuked the disciples for eating in public.
options.note: He defended the disciples and answered the Pharisees, not the disciples.

quiz.q: What principle did Jesus teach by healing the man with the withered hand?

options.text: It is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, for a person is more valuable than a sheep.
options.note: Verses 11-12 establish that mercy and doing good honor the Sabbath.

options.text: Healing should be postponed until after the Sabbath.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus healed then and there, teaching it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.

options.text: Only priests may heal on the Sabbath.
options.note: Jesus makes no such restriction; He teaches that doing good is always lawful.

options.text: The Sabbath forbids all activity of any kind.
options.note: Jesus shows the Sabbath is for mercy and doing good, not rigid inactivity.

quiz.q: How did the Pharisees respond to Jesus' Sabbath healing?

options.text: They went out and plotted how they might kill Him.
options.note: Verse 14 records the plot against His life.

options.text: They admitted He was right and repented.
options.note: The opposite; they hardened into a murderous plot rather than repenting.

options.text: They asked Him to teach them more about the Sabbath.
options.note: They did not seek His teaching; they conspired against Him.

options.text: They celebrated the man's healing with the crowd.
options.note: Far from celebrating, they plotted to kill Jesus.

quiz.q: How does Matthew describe Jesus through the Isaiah quotation?

options.text: As the gentle, chosen Servant who will not break a bruised reed and brings hope to the nations.
options.note: Verses 18-21 quote Isaiah 42, portraying the tender, Spirit-anointed Servant.

options.text: As a conquering warrior who crushes His enemies at once.
options.note: He will lead justice to victory, but the emphasis is His gentleness with the weak, not immediate conquest.

options.text: As a loud public agitator stirring the crowds.
options.note: The Servant will not quarrel or cry out in the streets; the picture is quiet gentleness.

options.text: As a Servant sent only to Israel, never the nations.
options.note: The quotation says the nations will hope in His name, extending His mission beyond Israel.

quiz.q: What does the whole passage reveal about Jesus?

options.text: He is Lord of the Sabbath and the gentle Servant, restoring mercy and bringing hope to the nations.
options.note: The Sabbath authority and the Servant prophecy together define His identity and mission.

options.text: He is chiefly a teacher of stricter Sabbath rules.
options.note: He is Lord of the Sabbath who recovers mercy, not a teacher of stricter rules.

options.text: He is a rebel bent on abolishing God's law.
options.note: He upholds the law's true intent and claims authority over it, not abolition.

options.text: He is a harsh judge with no compassion for the weak.
options.note: The Servant will not break the bruised reed; He is gentle with the weak.

questions: Jesus said God desires mercy, not sacrifice. Where might you be prizing rules or appearances over showing genuine mercy to people?
The Pharisees watched Jesus in order to accuse Him, while He watched the man in order to heal him. Whose posture is more like yours toward people who are struggling?
Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and gives rest to the weary. How are you resting in Him rather than in your own performance or religious effort?
The Servant will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick. How does Jesus' gentleness with the weak and faltering meet you where you feel fragile today?
Even under threat, Jesus responded with quiet mercy rather than retaliation. Where is God calling you to answer hostility with gentleness rather than striking back?

translationNotes.note: The consecrated bread is the Bread of the Presence, Leviticus 24:5-9, reserved for the priests, which David and his men nonetheless ate in their need.
I desire mercy, not sacrifice quotes Hosea 6:6, the same text Jesus cited in Matthew 9:13, exposing the leaders' loveless legalism.
This is Isaiah 42:1-4, the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew, presenting Jesus as the gentle, Spirit-anointed Servant who brings justice and hope to the nations.
